# The name Yongwang and the world it opens

A name is a door. **Yongwang** opens onto ​the domain of dragon king, sea, the Korean tradition, and centuries of storytelling, worship, and scholarship. This post moves through that world room by room — the name and its roots, the ‌original script, the sound of it, the myths, the symbols, the sites, and its afterlife — before arriving at the digital temple that makes the record addressable. The letters are plain; the ‌evidence is not.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Yongwang
- **ASCII form:** yongwang
- **Meaning:** "Dragon king"
- **Domain of influence:** Dragon King, Sea
- **Pantheon:** Korean
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** 용왕 (龍王) (Hangul + ​Hanja)

## Overview

**Yongwang** (*yongwang*) — Dragon King, Sea · Ruler of rivers, seas, and rain — belongs to the Korean tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Dragon King, Sea". The ​name means "Dragon king".

Yongwang — 龍王, “dragon king” — is the sovereign of the Korean seas: master of storms, rain, and the shoals of fish on which coastal villages live. Reached ​through Buddhist liturgy, shamanic gut ritual, and village folktale alike, he rewards respect with calm water and punishes neglect with empty nets and sudden gale.

The name is attested in Hangul + Hanja as **용왕 (龍王)**. Etymologically it means ‌"Dragon king".

The canonical spelling **Yongwang** matches the conventional scholarly romanization. ## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Hangul + Hanja as **용왕 (龍王)** — Korean alphabet + Chinese characters, ​attested Modern Korean, in Korea. The script is written left-to-right.

The scholarly transliteration is *Yongwang* (Revised Romanization), giving the normalized reading /joŋ.waŋ/.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Hangul 용왕 with Hanja ‌龍王 — the Dragon King of the waters

Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For **Yongwang**, the Hangul form ​is **용왕** and the Hanja form is **龍王**. Hangul ‘용왕’ and Hanja ‘龍王’; the figure is shared with East Asian dragon-king traditions but has distinct Korean cultic forms. The ASCII form *yongwang* ‌is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration **Yongwang** is the scholarly citation form.

## Pronunciation

The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/joŋ.waŋ/** — Korean Reconstruction.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **joŋ** — The first syllable ​of Yongwang, carrying primary stress in the romanised form.
- **waŋ** — The middle syllable or element, pronounced with level pitch in Korean.
- **-** — The final syllable, often closing in a nasal ​or simple vowel in the Korean reading.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'YOHNG-wahng' — Both syllables end in velar nasals. The name is the Sino-Korean title for the dragon ​king, ruler of the seas.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Hangul** — 용왕 — the Korean script form.
- **Hanja** — 龍王 — the Sino-Korean character form.

Both syllables end in ​velar nasals. The name is the Sino-Korean title for the dragon king, ruler of the seas.

## Mythology

The mythology of Yongwang is preserved in Korean oral tradition, shamanic ritual texts, and classical ​sources such as the Samguk Yusa. The narratives are not merely stories; they encode social values, ritual obligations, and relationships between humans, nature, and the sacred. Some details vary by region and ‌by shamanic lineage.

### The Underwater Palace (Sea cult)

Yongwang is believed to live in a magnificent palace beneath the sea, where he keeps treasures, controls the tides, and commands armies of fish, ​turtles, and dragons. Fishermen who offended Yongwang risked storms and empty nets.

### The Yongwang-gut (Ritual)

Coastal communities held Yongwang-gut, shamanic rituals dedicated to the dragon king. Offerings of rice, fruit, and specially ‌prepared food were set afloat or presented on the shore to secure calm seas and abundant catches.

### The Visitor to the Dragon King (Folktale)

Korean folktales sometimes tell of a poor but virtuous ​person who is carried to Yongwang's palace and rewarded with a magical gift. Such stories teach respect for the sea and warn against greed.

### The Python and the Wish-Jewel (Folktale)

The Samguk ‌Yusa, “Memorabilia of the Three Kingdoms” (13th century), tells of a poor but kind-hearted man who gave shelter to a strange traveller caught by night and rain. The stranger revealed himself as ​an imugi — a python that had waited a thousand years for the yeouiju, the wish-granting jewel that alone can raise a serpent to dragonhood. Entrusting the jewel to his host, the ‌imugi attempted the ascent to heaven; when it slipped, the man caught it and set it upon the serpent’s head, and the imugi became a true dragon and rose into the sky. ​In gratitude the dragon left a bright band of his own body coiled around the man’s house as a blessing, and the Samguk Yusa says this is why Koreans paint banded, rainbow ‌colours along the eaves of their houses to this day. The tale teaches that the sea’s greatest power answers to ordinary human kindness — and that even a dragon’s fortune once depended ​on a stranger’s open door.

### The King Who Became a Dragon (Royal cult)

The Samguk Sagi and Samguk Yusa record that King Munmu of Silla (r. 661–681), dying, commanded that his body ​be cremated and the ashes cast into the East Sea. “I will become a dragon,” he said, “and protect this kingdom from the pirates of the east.” His queen and son fulfilled the ‌vow; the ashes were committed to the sea off the coast near Gampo, and his son King Sinmun raised above the shore the temple Gameunsa — “the temple that appeases the sea” ‌— whose pagodas still stand at Gyeongju. The episode makes explicit what coastal religion had long implied: that the Dragon King and the dead king could share one body, and that the ‌sea’s protection was a royal responsibility, paid for in flesh. Korean Buddhists still honour Munmu as the dragon of the East Sea; the tale binds kingship, Buddhism, and the sea into a ​single sacred geography.

### The Yongwang-gut of the Fishing Villages (Ritual)

In the fishing villages of Korea’s south coast — Chaeseon in Tongyeong, Suyeong in Busan — shamans performed the Yongwang-gut, the rite ​of the Dragon King, to open the fishing season and beg calm seas. The folklorist Im Seok-jae recorded these rites in the twentieth century, when they were already old: the shaman invokes ‌the dragon kings of the four seas in turn, receives their possessing presence, and sends a paper dragon-boat laden with rice, fruit, cloth, and coins out onto the water, the offering itself ​sailing to the palace beneath the waves. If the season proves good, the debt is remembered; if storms come, the rite is repeated with greater care. Here mythology is not a story ​but a contract renewed each year — a working relationship between a fishing people and the sovereign of the deep, maintained with drum, cymbal, and a boat far too small for its cargo ‌of gratitude.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with Yongwang concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Dragon** — The serpentine sovereign of water ​and weather.
- **Waves** — The visible form of Yongwang's domain and power.
- **Pearl** — The luminous treasure of the underwater palace, symbolising wisdom and bounty.
- **Turtle** — A messenger and attendant of ​the dragon king who connects land and sea.

- **Pearl (yeouiju)** — The wish-granting jewel of the underwater palace — the treasure for which a python waits a thousand years.

## Archaeology & Evidence

‌No monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus is yet assigned to Yongwang with certainty. That absence should be read honestly: for a Korean name of this type the material ​record is expected to be thin, and the primary evidence remains the textual testimony gathered in the Scholarly Sources section.

Were such evidence to surface, it would take recognizable forms: votive or ‌dedicatory inscriptions naming 용왕 (龍王), sanctuary or cult remains tied to dragon king and iconography matching its traditional attributes (dragon and waves). Each candidate would be weighed against the reconstructed form of ​the name before entering the scholarly record.

## Realm & Domain

**Yongwang** is the dragon king, ruler of the seas and controller of rain, storms, and the waters upon which human life depends ​in Korean tradition. The name means "Dragon king" and belongs to the domain "Dragon King, Sea." Yongwang is the dragon king, a powerful deity of the sea who controls storms, rain, and the ​abundance of fish. He is worshipped especially in coastal fishing communities, where rituals ask for safe voyages and plentiful catches.

### Dragon King

Yongwang rules the seas as a royal dragon of immense ​power.

### Ruler of Seas

He governs tides, currents, and the creatures of the deep.

### Rain and Storms

The dragon king controls the weather that brings both life and destruction.

### Fisherfolk Protector

Coastal ‌communities depend on Yongwang for safe voyages and abundant fish.

## Across Cultures

Yongwang is part of a broader East Asian dragon-king tradition, with close parallels in Chinese, Japanese, and Vietnamese religion. In ‌Korea the figure was absorbed into both Buddhism and shamanism, appearing as a donor or protector in Buddhist temples and as a sovereign spirit in gut rituals. Daoist cosmology supplied iconography and ​ritual methods for invoking rain. Despite these borrowings, the Korean Yongwang has a distinctive local colouring tied to fishing villages, coastal geography, and the hazards of the Korea Strait.

Kindred figures in ‌the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[longwang|Lóngwáng]] (same figure, two traditions), [[aseratu|Ašeratu]] (sea / water), [[babaluaye|Ọbalúayé]] (sea / water), [[benzaiten|Benzaiten]] (sea / water), [[ea|Ēa]] (sea / water), and [[hoderi|Hoderi]] (sea / water).

## Cultural ​Legacy

Yongwang remains a vivid figure in Korean coastal culture, appearing in temple art, village rituals, seafood markets, and popular media. Dragon king imagery decorates boats, restaurants, and festivals, and prayers for ​safe fishing continue in many communities. The figure also influences Korean environmental thought, serving as a symbol of the sea's power and the need for respectful relations with marine ecosystems. In games and ‌animation, Yongwang often appears as a majestic dragon lord.

## A Meditation

Yongwang embodies the oldest human bargain with the ‌sea: reverence in exchange for survival. The ocean that feeds Korea can erase it in a night, and the Dragon King gives that double truth a face, a palace, and a name. ​He is what a fishing people build when they cannot control the water but cannot leave it either — a sovereign to whom gratitude, offerings, and good behaviour can be addressed. In ‌him the natural and the political also fuse: a king of Silla becomes a dragon to guard the coast, because protecting the realm at sea was understood as the same office as ​protecting it on land. To study Yongwang is to study how religion works at its most practical: not to explain the storm, but to negotiate with it — year after year, in ​the only coin a dragon accepts, ceremony.
